questions.question:
I traced the actual getting-started path for your Python ML engineer persona. Here's what I think they experience today — does this match reality?

---

T+0:00  Opens README. Clear: `pip install evalkit==2.0.0b1`, set EVALKIT_API_KEY.
T+1:30  Follows next instruction: `python examples/first_eval.py`. FileNotFoundError. The file is not in the package. README lied.
T+2:00  Searches the package for another entry point. Finds `python -m evalkit.demo`.
T+2:30  Runs it. It starts. Nothing prints.
T+3:00  Still nothing. No progress indicator. No timeout message. Wonders if it crashed.
T+6:00  A score finally appears. The SDK was running a silent 5-minute remote CI check nobody warned them about.
T+6:30  Tries `run_eval(dataset, evaluator)` in their own code.
T+7:00  Accidentally calls `run_batch(evaluator, dataset)` — same concept, flipped order, silent wrong results.
T+8:00  Passes a bad API key. Gets `AuthError: request failed`. No cause. No fix. Googles it.
T+10:00 Upgrades from v1. `Client.evaluate()` raises AttributeError. No migration guide found. Files a GitHub issue.

---

Where am I wrong, if anywhere?

options.label: Accurate — proceed (Recommended)
options.description: This matches the real getting-started experience. Use this as the basis for the review.

options.label: Mostly right, minor corrections
options.description: The broad strokes are right but some details are off. I'll note corrections.

options.label: Significantly off — actual experience differs
options.description: The narrative doesn't reflect reality. I'll describe the actual path.

questions.question:
D1 — Journey stage: Hello World (T+1:30 failure)

The README says: “follow the quickstart’s command: `python examples/first_eval.py`”
But docs/package-contents.txt confirms `examples/first_eval.py` is absent from both the published package and the release examples archive.

Every new developer hits a FileNotFoundError at minute 1.5, before they’ve gotten any value. This is a T=0 trust-breaker — the first instruction in the README doesn’t work. DX Principle: Zero Friction at T0.

Recommendation: A — update README to point to `python -m evalkit.demo` as the primary quickstart, because the demo module IS in the package and already produces real scores. Adding the missing file risks scope creep (examples need to be kept in sync).
Completeness: A=9/10, B=8/10, C=6/10

options.label: A: Fix README to point to demo (Recommended)
options.description: Change README.md: replace `python examples/first_eval.py` with `python -m evalkit.demo` as the primary quickstart command. One-line fix, consistent with the settled demo delivery vehicle.

options.label: B: Add examples/first_eval.py to the package
options.description: Include the missing file in the published package. Works, but requires writing and maintaining a quickstart script that mirrors the demo.

options.label: C: Add note that file requires separate download
options.description: Document that examples/ is a separate archive, not in the pip package. Reduces the surprise but doesn’t eliminate the friction.

answers.D1 — Journey stage: Hello World (T+1:30: A: Fix README to point to demo (Recommended)

questions.question:
D2 — Journey stage: Hello World / Demo (T+2:30–6:00 silence)

The demo runs `python -m evalkit.demo`. But docs/current-contracts.md says: “On a developer’s first local evaluation, the SDK requires a successful remote CI check and blocks for five minutes before returning an evaluation result. There is no skip flag or offline first-run path.”

This means the demo — the settled magical moment — also blocks for 5 minutes on first run, with no output, no progress, no ETA. The agreed TTHW target is <2 minutes (Champion tier). The current TTHW is 6 minutes (Red Flag tier). The gap is not closeable without changing this gate.

DX Principle: Zero Friction at T0. Fight Uncertainty (developer doesn’t know if it crashed).

Recommendation: B — exempt `python -m evalkit.demo` from the CI gate, because the demo uses bundled sample data that requires no remote validation. The CI gate makes sense for real evaluations; it does not apply to a canned demo.
Completeness: A=9/10, B=9/10, C=7/10

options.label: A: Add EVALKIT_SKIP_CI_CHECK env var / --no-ci flag (Recommended)
options.description: Add an escape hatch for local development. Developers set the env var to skip the gate. Production CI keeps the gate. Two lines of implementation.

options.label: B: Exempt python -m evalkit.demo from CI gate
options.description: The demo uses bundled data; CI check is meaningless for it. Exempt only the demo entrypoint. Smallest scope change that achieves <2-min TTHW for the first-run experience.

options.label: C: Add a progress indicator during the CI wait
options.description: Keep the 5-minute gate but print a progress message every 30s. Eliminates the ‘did it crash?’ confusion but doesn’t fix the 6-min TTHW. Still Red Flag tier.

options.label: D: Accept current behavior — defer TTHW to post-beta
options.description: Acknowledge the gap in the plan but defer the fix. Current TTHW stays at 6 min; competitive position stays at Red Flag tier until after beta.

answers.D2 — Journey stage: Hello World / Demo (: A: Add EVALKIT_SKIP_CI_CHECK env var / --no-ci flag (Recommended)

questions.question:
D3 — Journey stage: Debug (T+8:00)

The developer passes a bad API key. docs/api.md documents the current behavior: `AuthError("request failed")`. The plan retains this message. Per the same file: “There is no authentication error code, explanation of the cause, or instruction for replacing the key.”

All other errors in the SDK already identify cause, argument, and actionable fix (per docs/current-contracts.md). The auth error is the only outlier.

What the developer sees: `AuthError: request failed`. What they think: “Did the network fail? Is the API down? Is my key expired? Is it the wrong format?” They Google it. Context switching: 10-20 minutes lost.

DX Principle: Fight Uncertainty. Every error = problem + cause + fix.

Recommendation: A — rewrite the message with cause + fix + code. It’s consistent with every other error in the SDK and costs a single string change.
Completeness: A=10/10, B=7/10

options.label: A: Rewrite auth error with cause + fix + code (Recommended)
options.description: Change to: `AuthError("Invalid API key — EVALKIT_API_KEY is missing, expired, or incorrect. Generate a new key at https://evalkit.io/dashboard/keys", code=\"auth_invalid_key\")`. One string change; consistent with all other SDK errors.

options.label: B: Add error code only, keep current message
options.description: Add `code=\"auth_invalid_key\"` to the existing `AuthError(\"request failed\")`. Structured-API consumers can branch on it; CLI users still see an opaque message.

answers.D3 — Journey stage: Debug (T+8:00)\n\nTh: A: Rewrite auth error with cause + fix + code (Recommended)

questions.question:
D4 — Journey stage: Real Usage (silent wrong results)

The two core evaluation functions have reversed positional order:
  run_eval(dataset, evaluator)   ← dataset first
  run_batch(evaluator, dataset)  ← evaluator first

Both argument names describe the same concepts. docs/api.md notes: “The reversed positional order is intentional in the current draft; neither function requires keyword arguments.”

A developer who learns `run_eval` and then calls `run_batch` will pass arguments in the wrong order. No type error fires (both args accept similar types). They get wrong results silently.

DX Principle: Decide for me, let me override. API consistency is a trust signal.

Recommendation: A — standardize to `(dataset, evaluator)` order for both. Breaking change, but both functions are new in v2 (no existing callers to migrate). This is the cheapest moment to fix the inconsistency.
Completeness: A=10/10, B=8/10, C=6/10

options.label: A: Standardize to (dataset, evaluator) for both (Recommended)
options.description: Flip run_batch to match run_eval. Both functions are v2-new, so no existing call sites to migrate. Consistent API from day one.

options.label: B: Require keyword arguments for both
options.description: Add keyword-only enforcement: `run_eval(*, dataset, evaluator)` and `run_batch(*, evaluator, dataset)`. Callers must name args; wrong order is a TypeError. Keeps current naming.

options.label: C: Document the asymmetry clearly, leave as-is
options.description: Add a prominent warning in the docs. Asymmetry stays; documentation burden is on the user. Some developers will still get it wrong.

answers.D4 — Journey stage: Real Usage (silent w: A: Standardize to (dataset, evaluator) for both (Recommended)

questions.question:
D5 — Journey stage: Upgrade (AttributeError with no guidance)

Version 1 exposes `Client.evaluate()`. Version 2 replaces it with `Client.run()` and removes the old name immediately. Per docs/api.md: “No compatibility alias, deprecation warning, migration guide, or codemod is provided.”

A v1 developer who upgrades gets `AttributeError: 'Client' object has no attribute 'evaluate'` with no suggestion of what to use instead. They either stay on v1 or file an issue.

DX Principle: Credible — developers need to upgrade without fear. Upgrade fear is a real adoption blocker: if upgrading breaks things silently, developers stay pinned to old versions.

Recommendation: A — add a deprecation shim in the beta, because it costs 3 lines and eliminates a hard break for every v1 user. A shim in beta that prints a warning (not an error) gives users a runway before the shim is removed in v3.
Completeness: A=9/10, B=7/10, C=6/10

options.label: A: Add Client.evaluate() deprecation shim (Recommended)
options.description: Add `Client.evaluate = deprecated_alias(Client.run)` that calls `Client.run()` and emits a DeprecationWarning: “evaluate() removed in v2; use run() instead.” Remove in v3. 3-line change; zero breakage for v1 users on upgrade.

options.label: B: Add a one-page migration guide (no shim)
options.description: Write docs/migration-v1-v2.md with a sed or ast-grep codemod snippet. No backward compat alias. Developers must update call sites manually but have clear instructions.

options.label: C: Accept hard break, document in changelog only
options.description: The changelog already notes the removal. No new code or docs. v1 developers get an AttributeError and must find the changelog entry themselves.

questions.question:
D6 — Pass 4: Documentation (expected output missing from README)

After D1, the README quickstart becomes: `python -m evalkit.demo`. But the README doesn’t show what output to expect. The developer runs the demo, waits ~1 minute, and doesn’t know if it’s working or what success looks like until a score appears.

Showing a 3-4 line output snippet in the README (the kind of thing `python -m evalkit.demo` actually prints) gives developers a clear success signal without reading any more docs.

DX Principle: Fight Uncertainty. Zero Friction at T0.

Recommendation: A — add expected output to the README because it costs 3 lines and eliminates the ‘is this working?’ anxiety during the wait.
Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score.

options.label: A: Add expected output snippet to README (Recommended)
options.description: Append 3-4 lines of sample output below the quickstart command so developers know what success looks like before running. E.g. `Evaluating 10 samples... Score: 0.84 | Pass: 8/10 | Fail: 2/10`

options.label: B: Skip — output is self-evident from running the demo
options.description: The demo prints real scores; developers will see the output immediately. Showing it in advance adds noise to the README.

answers.D6 — Pass 4: Documentation (expected out: A: Add expected output snippet to README (Recommended)

questions.question:
D7 — Pass 5: Upgrade Path (migration guide to complement the D5 shim)

D5 adds `Client.evaluate()` as a DeprecationWarning shim. A developer will see: `DeprecationWarning: evaluate() removed in v2; use run() instead.` That’s a good runtime signal.

But a developer reading the changelog or docs before upgrading has no guidance: no before/after example, no list of renamed symbols, no one-line codemod. A short migration note in the changelog or a new `docs/migration-v1-v2.md` gives them confidence before they even try `pip install evalkit==2.0.0b1`.

DX Principle: Credible. Upgrade fear blocks adoption.

Recommendation: A — add a brief migration note because it’s 5 lines in the changelog and eliminates upgrade hesitation for current v1 users.
Completeness: A=9/10, B=8/10

options.label: A: Add brief migration note to changelog (Recommended)
options.description: Add a “Migrating from v1” subsection to the existing changelog: list the rename (`evaluate()` → `run()`), confirm everything else is unchanged, include a one-liner sed codemod. ~5 lines.

options.label: B: Shim is sufficient — skip extra docs
options.description: The DeprecationWarning from D5 tells developers what to do at runtime. Additional docs are extra maintenance surface.

answers.D7 — Pass 5: Upgrade Path (migration gui: A: Add brief migration note to changelog (Recommended)

questions.question:
TODO candidate: Progress indicator during the first-run CI wait

D2 added EVALKIT_SKIP_CI_CHECK for local dev. But when that flag is NOT set — in a developer’s own CI pipeline, or when they don’t know about the flag — the SDK still blocks for 5 minutes with no output. A progress message every 30s (“Waiting for CI check... 90s elapsed”) eliminates the ‘did it crash?’ confusion without changing the gate behavior.

What: Print a progress line to stderr every 30s during the CI wait.
Why: Without it, non-skip path users see 5 minutes of silence.
Pros: Eliminates uncertainty on the non-skip path; 10 lines of code.
Cons: Adds noise to CI logs if the user pipes stdout.
Depends on: D2 (skip flag) is already resolved.

options.label: A: Add to this plan (ship with beta) (Recommended)
options.description: Add a 30s progress stderr printer to the CI wait loop. Part of the beta polish scope.

options.label: B: Defer to post-beta TODO
options.description: Log it as a follow-up. Skip flag covers local dev; progress indicator is a quality-of-life improvement for later.

options.label: C: Skip entirely
options.description: The skip flag is sufficient. Non-skip path developers see CI logs anyway.

answers.TODO candidate: Progress indicator durin: A: Add to this plan (ship with beta) (Recommended)

questions.question:
TODO candidate: Exempt python -m evalkit.demo from the CI gate (no env var needed)

D2 added EVALKIT_SKIP_CI_CHECK so developers can bypass the first-run CI check. But the optimal UX for the demo is zero-friction with no flags or env vars. Since `python -m evalkit.demo` uses bundled sample data and no real API calls, the CI check is meaningless for it regardless of settings.

What: In evalkit/demo.py, detect the demo entrypoint and skip the CI check unconditionally.
Why: `python -m evalkit.demo` should always work in <1 minute, even for developers who don’t know about EVALKIT_SKIP_CI_CHECK.
Pros: Zero-friction demo path; consistent with the “no hosted service” promise; 2 lines of code.
Cons: Two places that bypass the CI gate (env var + demo module) could confuse developers who expect gate parity.
Depends on: D2 (skip flag) and D1 (README points to demo) already resolved.

options.label: A: Add to this plan (ship with beta) (Recommended)
options.description: Exempt python -m evalkit.demo from the CI gate unconditionally. The demo entrypoint uses bundled data; the gate is irrelevant.

options.label: B: Defer — env var is sufficient for beta
options.description: The EVALKIT_SKIP_CI_CHECK env var already handles this for informed developers. The demo exemption is a quality-of-life improvement; defer to post-beta.

options.label: C: Skip — keep gate parity
options.description: All first evaluations should go through the CI gate, including the demo. Consistency > convenience here.
